checkpoints: The handler writes the post and returns 201 immediately, without waiting for fanout to complete.

Instead of computing fanout inline, the handler enqueues a fanout job onto a queue — a separate worker owns resolving followers and writing timelines entirely on its own, fully detached from the request path.

The job payload carries only postId, authorId, and createdAt/sortOrder — just enough for the worker to redo the whole job on its own (postId identifies the post, authorId resolves the follower list via the follows table, createdAt/sortOrder preserves write order).
Below the follower-count threshold, the worker takes the push branch: it resolves the followers and writes pushed_timeline in batches for each of them.
Above the threshold, the worker skips fanout entirely for that post, leaving that author (a KOL/celebrity) to the pull path at read time.
Fanout is made idempotent via a unique (postId, userId) key in pushed_timeline, so a retried/redelivered job is a no-op rather than duplicating an entry.
Each timeline is bounded — trimmed to the latest N entries after every fanout — so storage doesn't grow unbounded; older history is served by the pull path instead.
The design deliberately accepts eventual consistency (a follower may see the new post a few seconds late) as the price for fast, decoupled post creation.
The interface is route(authorId) → { route: 'push' | 'pull', expectedWrites }, deciding off a classification signal — the isCelebrity flag or a follower count — read from the authors table.
expectedWrites is 1 when the route is pull (author pulled at read time), or the follower count when the route is push — exposing the actual write-amplification signal of the decision.
The module has exactly ONE responsibility — answer 'which route' — not execute the fanout or the merge itself.
Both the write path (fanout-on-write decision) and the read path (pull-and-merge decision) call into the same route() function, so the push/pull decision has exactly one source of truth.

The celebrity threshold should never be a hardcoded constant in code — it must be an operational knob, since it depends on Redis write capacity, the fanout queue's latency SLA, and the author's posting frequency, tuned by starting with an estimate and monitoring for drift.
On push→pull migration (author crosses threshold), old push rows scattered across followers' feeds must either TTL-expire or be swept by an explicit cleanup job.
On pull→push migration (author drops below threshold), the feed must be warmed/backfilled, since followers' feeds never held that author's posts via push before.
During the transition window, while old push rows and the new pull path briefly coexist, merging must dedup by postId to avoid a post showing up twice.
The isCelebrity flag, read from Postgres, is the entire rule that routePost() branches on and nothing else.
kol_1 (isCelebrity: true) routes to pull-at-read-time with expectedWrites: 1 — the post is written exactly once, and every follower pulls it at feed-read time.
author_1 (isCelebrity: false) routes to push-to-followers with expectedWrites: number_of_followers — the post is written once per follower, right away.
Pushing a celebrity's post to its hundreds of thousands of followers within seconds would trigger exactly the write-amplification storm that split-routing exists to avoid.
For a normal author, that per-follower write cost is small enough to be worth paying for the fast, pre-built read every follower then gets.
Hybrid fanout is not the system picking push or pull as a single strategy — it classifies each author and applies whichever strategy fits that author.
The push timeline and the pull timeline are merged back together at read time, so the follower never notices the two posts took completely different paths to get there.
This is classic offset drift: rank-based pagination assumes the underlying set stays put between two reads, but a realtime feed keeps getting new posts ZADDed into the ZSET.
ZREVRANGE key 0 19 takes the 20 highest-rank elements for page 1; when 5 new higher-scored posts slot in, the rank of all 20 already-read posts shifts down by exactly 5.
Page 2's ZREVRANGE key 20 39 has no idea that shift happened, so range 20..39 now overlaps the last 5 posts of page 1 plus the front of what should be page 2's own posts — the user sees duplicates.
The fix drops the position-counting offset and switches to a cursor pinned to a concrete data value: lastScore, the score of the last item the previous page returned.
The next page reads via ZREVRANGEBYSCORE key (lastScore)-1 -inf LIMIT 0 20.

Because new posts always score higher than lastScore, they sit above the cursor and never fall into the range the next read scans, so an insert at the head of the ZSET no longer skews anything below the cursor.
Page 1 (hot, low risk since it was just loaded) can keep using plain ZREVRANGE; only pagination from page 2 onward needs to switch to the score cursor.
Pure pull makes sense for read-light systems, feeds where correctness-right-now is critical, or workloads where follower counts are uniform across accounts.
Pull never amplifies write cost and always reflects the current state, since there is no physical timeline that can drift out of sync.
Its weakness is read fan-in: every request has to run a join across every author the user follows.
At peak (e.g. millions of people opening the feed at once at 8am), that fan-in load lands entirely on the database.
It is mitigated by indexing (authorId, createdAt), capping the query's time window, and caching hot pull results.
The cache itself is already a materialized layer, so pushing pull mitigation far enough reconstructs the very hybrid architecture you were trying to avoid.
The pull-versus-hybrid decision is a function of read/write ratio and follower distribution, not a fixed rule — pull is right until read fan-in starts to dominate.

Cache warming pays its cost at write time so every read stays a plain ZREVRANGE against an already-materialized ZSET — great for a user who opens their feed constantly, because they never eat a cold-start rebuild.

The price of warming is fanning one publish out into every follower's feed:{followerId} via ZADD, one call per follower: cheap for a normal author, but a celebrity with millions of followers turns a single post into millions of ZSET writes.
This is the exact write amplification the lesson already flags for fanout-on-write, just happening at the Redis cache layer instead of the database layer.

On-demand materialization is the mirror image: publish stays a single Postgres insert, nothing touches Redis, and seedTimeline only rebuilds a user's ZSET the moment they actually request their feed — cheap everywhere except the first read after a cold start or eviction, which now carries the full rebuild that warming would have paid earlier.

Neither strategy is universally right, so the senior move is to blend them by who the user actually is: warm the ZSETs of hot, frequently-active users, since the read-latency win there is worth the write cost.
Leave cold or dormant users on the on-demand path this lesson implements, since pre-warming a feed nobody opens just burns writes for nothing.

Keep celebrity authors off the warming path entirely regardless of their followers' activity, routing their posts through on-demand or a merge-at-read step instead, so one post never fans out into millions of writes.
This is not a new trade-off — it is the same push-vs-pull decision the module already makes at the fanout layer, just relocated to whether the cache gets filled proactively or lazily.
Routing a KOL to pull only solves the write side — the post is now written once instead of fanning out to hundreds of thousands of feeds.

The read side is not solved yet: that KOL's cached timeline still lives on a single Redis key, and because Redis serves each slot single-threaded, a huge crowd of followers reading that key almost simultaneously turns it into a hotkey, bottlenecking every other request landing on the same slot, not just requests for this KOL.
Key-salting fixes it by splitting one key into N keys feed:kol:{authorId}:salt:0..N-1 (N=4 in the current code), with the salt computed deterministically from userId.charCodeAt(len-1) % 4.

The same userId always maps to one fixed slot, keeping cache-hit behavior stable per user, while the crowd of hundreds of thousands of followers spreads evenly across the N slots, turning one bottleneck into N lighter-loaded points.
In exchange, the KOL's cache is duplicated up to N times, meaning N times the memory.
Every time the KOL posts, the system must update/invalidate all N keys instead of one.

On Redis Cluster, attaching an {authorId} hash tag to co-locate all N salts on one slot for a convenient batched MGET accidentally collapses them back onto one node, undoing the very spreading you salted for.
Salting is not a free lunch: it trades memory and write cost for read throughput, and on Cluster you additionally have to weigh locality against distribution.

A synchronous `for` loop that `await`s a per-follower database write inside an HTTP request handler makes that handler's latency scale linearly with follower count, since every write must finish before a response can be sent.

When the same unconditional code path handles both a 2-follower author and a millions-of-followers celebrity, the only variable separating an instant response from a multi-minute timeout is how many rows the follower lookup returns — there is no branch that treats the two cases differently.

Fanout work belongs off the request path: persisting the post and returning 201 immediately, then enqueuing a fanout job for a separate background worker to drain, decouples response latency from follower count entirely.

A follower-count gate is a second, independent fix from moving fanout off the request path — below a threshold the push-on-write job still enqueues normally, but above it fanout is skipped entirely and that author's posts are served through the pull path (joining follows and posts at read time) instead.

Fixing only one of the two causes leaves a real hole: async-only still lets a celebrity's fanout burn worker capacity writing millions of rows that may go unread, while gating-only still blocks the request of an author with a few thousand followers.

Write amplification — one post turning into N per-follower timeline writes — is the underlying mechanism driving both the timeout and the cost of unconditional fanout, and it is what the async/gate fixes are designed to control.

Deferring fanout to a background worker introduces eventual consistency (a follower's timeline row appears a few seconds after the post, not instantly), which is an acceptable trade-off for a feed rather than a correctness regression.

A background fanout worker must be idempotent, for example by upserting on a `(userId, postId)` primary key, so that a retried or redelivered job cannot insert a duplicate timeline row for the same follower.
A Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) keeps its members ordered strictly by their numeric score inside an internal skip list, and ZREVRANGE simply walks that skip list from the high end to the low end.

Because ZREVRANGE has no concept of "recency" on its own, the order it returns is entirely determined by whatever value was written as the score at insert time — if that value doesn't represent time, the output doesn't represent time either.

In seedTimeline, the score passed to zadd is `rank`, a loop counter that increments by exactly 1 on every row processed, rather than `row.scoreMs`, the real epoch-millisecond timestamp already available on each post.
Because `rank` only reflects the order rows came back from `this.posts.find({ order: { scoreMs: "ASC" } })`, the ZSET ends up sorted by seed/insertion order rather than by true chronological recency.

A post that is genuinely newer (larger real scoreMs) but happens to be seeded earlier in the loop receives a smaller rank value than an older post seeded later, so it sinks below that older post when the feed is read back.

getCachedFeed itself is correct: zrevrange(key, 0, 19, "WITHSCORES") reading the 20 highest-score members in descending order is exactly the intended read pattern for this cache; the defect is confined entirely to the write side in seedTimeline.

The fix is a one-line change — replace `rank` with `row.scoreMs` in the zadd call — so that a larger score corresponds to a later epoch timestamp, and the already-correct ZREVRANGE read then produces strict recency order.

Correctness after the fix should be verified by seeding posts in a shuffled, non-chronological order and asserting the returned timeline is strictly descending by real scoreMs/createdAt; two posts sharing the exact same scoreMs fall back to lexicographic ordering on postId inside the skip list, a separate edge case worth noting but not the bug itself.

Concatenating `pushedTimeline` and `celebrityPosts` without deduplicating by `id` breaks the moment an author is promoted from regular to KOL: both queries filter on the author's *current* celebrity flag rather than the flag at the time each post was written, so an author's older posts still sit in the push path while the same posts are now also pulled into the celebrity path, and every one of them renders twice in the merged feed.

The correct fix is a dedup pass keyed on `post.id` — for example building a `Map<string, Post>` or a `Set<string>` of seen ids while iterating the merged array and keeping only the first occurrence — applied right before the sort, not a change to either source query, since each query is individually correct and it is only the union that is wrong.

Because `this.getSaltedKolKey('kol_1', userId)` always passes the literal string `'kol_1'` instead of the celebrity's real `authorId`, every celebrity's cache is written and read under the exact same key family regardless of how many distinct KOLs exist in `celebrityIds`; once there is more than one celebrity, one celebrity's cache read can silently return another celebrity's cached timeline.

The fix for the salted-key bug is to pass the actual celebrity `authorId` being cached into `getSaltedKolKey` instead of a fixture id, and if the intent is one cache entry per KOL rather than one blended cache per reading user, cache each celebrity's timeline separately under its own real `authorId` and merge the cached results at read time instead of blending first and caching once under a shared identity.

Both the missing dedup and the hardcoded salted key are correctness bugs — the user is shown a wrong or cross-contaminated feed, not just a slow one — so they belong ahead of any cosmetic or stylistic PR comments and should be raised as blockers rather than nitpicks.

The tests passing and the demo timeline looking right prove nothing about the promotion case, since a single-snapshot dataset where no author's celebrity flag has ever changed can never exercise the stale-row overlap that causes the duplicate; the review has to explicitly reason about what happens the day an author crosses the threshold, not just about the code's current behavior.

A related but independent gap worth flagging is that nothing TTLs or deletes an author's stale push-timeline rows once they are promoted to celebrity, so even after the dedup fix lands, the duplicate-post problem keeps compounding on every future read unless a cleanup job or expiry handles the role-drift cleanup.

Concrete verification for these bugs means seeding an author as a regular user with existing posts, promoting them to celebrity, calling the hybrid feed, and asserting every `post.id` appears exactly once in the timeline; and separately seeding two distinct celebrities and asserting `getSaltedKolKey` resolves to two different keys rather than one shared key.
